title: Check Even or Odd
prompt: Write a function that determines if a given integer is even. Return True if it is even, and False if it is odd.

steps: Use the modulo operator to find the remainder when the number is divided by 2.
Check if this remainder is strictly equal to 0.
Return the resulting boolean value directly.
approach.example: For input 4, 4 % 2 is 0, which equals 0, returning True. For 7, 7 % 2 is 1, which does not equal 0, returning False.

code:
def is_even(num):
  return num % 2 == 0

walkthroughSteps: The modulo operator (%) performs integer division and returns the remainder.
All even numbers divide evenly by 2, leaving a remainder of exactly 0.
The comparison == 0 evaluates to True or False, which is immediately returned.
commonMistakes: Writing an if/else block to return True or False instead of just returning the boolean expression.
Using division (/) instead of modulo (%), which yields a float instead of a remainder.

title: FizzBuzz
prompt: Generate a list of strings representing numbers from 1 to n. Replace multiples of 3 with 'Fizz', multiples of 5 with 'Buzz', and multiples of both with 'FizzBuzz'.

steps: Initialize an empty list to hold the output strings.
Loop through all integers from 1 up to and including n.
Check if the number is divisible by 15 (both 3 and 5) first, appending 'FizzBuzz'.
Else check divisibility by 3 or 5 individually, appending the respective word.
If none apply, append the string representation of the number itself.
approach.example: For n=3, 1 is '1', 2 is '2', 3%3==0 is 'Fizz', returning ['1', '2', 'Fizz'].

walkthroughSteps: The result array is set up to accumulate the sequential string answers.
A for loop drives the iteration from 1 to the target n.
The modulo 15 check must come first, otherwise the modulo 3 check would intercept and incorrectly label 15 as just 'Fizz'.
Elif clauses ensure only one condition triggers per number.
The built-in str() function casts non-matching integers into strings.
commonMistakes: Placing the modulo 15 condition at the end of the if/elif chain, preventing it from ever being reached.
Appending the integer itself instead of converting it to a string first.

title: Two Sum
prompt: Given a list of numbers and a target integer, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Assume exactly one valid solution exists.

steps: Create an empty dictionary to map numbers to their indices.
Iterate over the list, tracking both the current index and the number.
Calculate the complement needed by subtracting the current number from the target.
Check if this complement already exists in the dictionary.
If it does, return the stored index and the current index; otherwise, add the current number to the dictionary.
approach.example: For [2, 7, 11, 15] target 9. index 0: num 2, complement 7, store {2:0}. index 1: num 7, complement 2. 2 is in dict at index 0. Return [0, 1].

walkthroughSteps: The dictionary 'seen' acts as a fast lookup table for values we have already passed.
Enumerate provides both the index 'i' and the value 'num' cleanly in one loop step.
The complement represents the exact value required to hit the target with the current 'num'.
Because dictionary key lookups are O(1), finding the complement is nearly instantaneous.
Recording the index of 'num' ensures future numbers can look backwards to find it.
commonMistakes: Using a nested loop to compare every possible pair, which creates a slow O(n^2) solution.
Adding the current number to the dictionary before checking for the complement, which can accidentally use the same number twice if target is 2*num.

title: Contains Duplicate
prompt: Determine if a list contains any duplicate values. Return True if any value appears at least twice, and False if every element is distinct.

steps: Initialize an empty set to keep track of numbers already encountered.
Iterate through each number in the input list.
If the current number is already in the set, a duplicate has been found, so return True.
If not, add the current number to the set.
If the loop finishes without finding any duplicates, return False.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 3, 1], add 1, add 2, add 3. Next is 1, which is already in the set. Return True.

walkthroughSteps: A set is created because sets provide O(1) average time complexity for both insertions and lookups.
The for loop systematically processes each element one by one.
The 'in' operator checks the set to see if the element was seen in previous iterations.
Finding a match triggers an immediate exit with True, saving time on early duplicate detection.
Only when the entire list consists of unique elements does the code reach the final False return.
commonMistakes: Using a list for 'seen' instead of a set, turning the O(n) algorithm into an O(n^2) algorithm.
Sorting the array first and comparing adjacent elements, which works but slows the time complexity to O(n log n).

title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
prompt: Given two sorted arrays of numbers, combine them into a single new sorted array and return it.

steps: Initialize an empty result array and two pointers starting at index 0 for both input arrays.
Loop while both pointers are within the bounds of their respective arrays.
Compare the elements at the two pointers, appending the smaller one to the result array and incrementing its pointer.
Once one array is exhausted, append all remaining elements from both arrays (only one will actually have elements left).
Return the merged array.
approach.example: For [1, 3] and [2]. 1 < 2, result=[1], p1=1. 3 > 2, result=[1, 2], p2=1. Second array exhausted. Append remaining from first, result=[1, 2, 3].

code:
def merge_sorted(arr1, arr2):
  result = []
  i = 0
  j = 0
  while i < len(arr1) and j < len(arr2):
    if arr1[i] < arr2[j]:
      result.append(arr1[i])
      i += 1
    else:
      result.append(arr2[j])
      j += 1
  result.extend(arr1[i:])
  result.extend(arr2[j:])
  return result

walkthroughSteps: The variables i and j track our current read position in arr1 and arr2, respectively.
The while loop ensures we don't try to access an index out of bounds in either array.
The comparison ensures the smallest available number is always added next, maintaining the sorted order.
The extend methods at the end cleanly scoop up any leftover elements after the while loop finishes.
Slicing with arr1[i:] is safe even if i is at the end of the list; it simply returns an empty list.
commonMistakes: Concatenating the arrays and calling sort(), which ignores the fact that they are already sorted and wastes time with O((n+m) log(n+m)).
Using a for loop over one array and searching the other, disrupting the optimal two-pointer flow.

title: Length of Last Word
prompt: Given a string consisting of words and spaces, return the length of the last valid word. A word is a maximal substring consisting of non-space characters only.

steps: Initialize a counter to track the length of the word.
Loop backwards through the string starting from the last character.
If a non-space character is encountered, increment the counter.
If a space is encountered and the counter is greater than zero, the last word is completely counted, so return the counter.
If the loop completes, return the counter.
approach.example: For 'Hello World  ', loop backwards. Skip spaces. Find 'd' (count 1), 'l' (2), 'r' (3), 'o' (4), 'W' (5). Find space, count is 5, return 5.

walkthroughSteps: The backwards loop avoids unnecessary processing of the entire string when we only care about the end.
The range uses -1 as the step and stops before -1 to cover index 0.
Trailing spaces are effectively ignored because the space condition does nothing until 'length' is greater than 0.
Once letters are found and counted, encountering a space triggers the elif branch to lock in the final length.
The fallback return handles strings that have no spaces at all or contain only a single word.
commonMistakes: Using text.split() and getting the last element, which takes O(n) auxiliary space to build the list of words.
Failing to account for trailing spaces at the very end of the string.

title: Valid Parentheses
prompt: Determine if a string of brackets '(', ')', '{', '}', '[', and ']' is valid. It is valid if open brackets are closed by the same type of brackets in the correct order.

steps: Initialize an empty list to act as a stack.
Create a dictionary mapping each closing bracket to its corresponding opening bracket.
Iterate through the characters in the string.
If it's an opening bracket, push it onto the stack. If it's a closing bracket, pop the top element from the stack (or use a dummy value if empty) and check if it matches the map.
Return True only if the loop completes and the stack is empty.
approach.example: For '{[]}', push '{', push '['. Encounter ']', pop '[' (matches). Encounter '}', pop '{' (matches). Stack empty, return True.

walkthroughSteps: The stack tracks unresolved opening brackets, ensuring the most recently opened bracket is closed first (LIFO order).
The dictionary provides rapid lookup to verify matching pairs.
Open brackets are identified by simply checking if the character is NOT a key in the bracket_map.
The pop safely handles empty stacks by assigning a dummy '#' character that will deliberately fail the match check.
Checking 'not stack' at the end ensures no opening brackets were left unmatched.
commonMistakes: Returning True immediately when a match is found instead of waiting to verify the entire string.
Forgetting to check if the stack is empty at the end, returning True for strings like '((('.

title: Search Insert Position
prompt: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index if the target is found. If not, return the index where it would be if it were inserted in order.

steps: Initialize two pointers, left at 0 and right at the end of the array.
Use a while loop to perform binary search as long as left is less than or equal to right.
Calculate the middle index.
If the middle element matches the target, return its index.
Adjust left or right pointers based on whether the target is larger or smaller than the middle element.
When the loop finishes without a match, the left pointer will be at the correct insertion index.
approach.example: For [1, 3, 5, 6] target 2. mid=1 (val 3). 2<3, right=0. mid=0 (val 1). 2>1, left=1. Loop ends. left is 1, return 1.

walkthroughSteps: The bounds left and right outline the active search space.
The floor division // cleanly calculates the midpoint integer.
Finding an exact match immediately returns the location mid.
Shifting left past mid or right before mid constantly cuts the search space in half, achieving logarithmic time.
Because of how the bounds cross, left invariably ends up pointing to the exact location where the target naturally fits.
commonMistakes: Using a linear scan (for loop) which operates in O(n) time, violating the optimal binary search approach.
Returning mid or right at the end of the loop instead of left, leading to off-by-one errors on insertion.

title: Plus One
prompt: You are given a large integer represented as an array of digits, where each element is a single digit. Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array.

steps: Traverse the array of digits backwards, starting from the last element.
If the current digit is 9, change it to 0 and continue to the next iteration (carrying the one).
If the current digit is not 9, add 1 to it and immediately return the array.
If the loop finishes, it means all digits were 9s (e.g., 999 becomes 000). Prepend a 1 to the array and return.
approach.example: For [1, 2, 9], last is 9, becomes 0. Next is 2, becomes 3. Return [1, 3, 0]. For [9], 9 becomes 0. Loop ends. Return [1, 0].

walkthroughSteps: Looping from right to left perfectly mimics manual addition math, prioritizing the least significant digit.
Changing 9s to 0s inherently handles the carry-over math for the next column.
If a digit isn't a 9, the addition simply finishes, and returning early saves unnecessary loop iterations.
The fallback return creates a new array dynamically for numbers like 99 -> 100, where the length increases.
commonMistakes: Converting the array to a single string, casting to an integer, adding 1, and casting back. This works but can fail on languages with integer size limits.
Failing to handle the edge case where every single digit is a 9, returning [0, 0] instead of [1, 0, 0].

title: Majority Element
prompt: Find the majority element in an array of size n. The majority element is the element that appears more than n / 2 times. Assume it always exists.

steps: Initialize a counter to 0 and a candidate variable to hold the potential majority element.
Iterate through the array.
If the counter is 0, assign the current element as the new candidate.
If the current element equals the candidate, increment the counter; otherwise, decrement the counter.
Return the candidate, which is guaranteed to be the majority element.
approach.example: For [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]: c=2, count=1 -> count=2 -> c=1, count=1 -> count=0 -> c=1, count=1 -> c=2, count=0 -> c=2, count=1. Return 2.

walkthroughSteps: This algorithm is known as Boyer-Moore Voting.
The 'count' variable tracks the net balance of the candidate compared to all other competing numbers.
When count hits 0, it means all previous elements have canceled each other out, so a new candidate is safely elected.
Because the majority element appears more than n/2 times, its count can never be permanently outvoted by all other elements combined.
The candidate standing at the end of the iteration is therefore the winner.
commonMistakes: Using a hash map to count all frequencies, which works but uses O(n) space instead of the optimal O(1).
Sorting the array to return the middle element. This is correct and takes O(1) space, but runs slower at O(n log n) time.

title: Single Number
prompt: Given a non-empty array of integers where every element appears twice except for one, find that single one. You must implement a solution with a linear runtime complexity and use only constant extra space.

steps: Initialize a result variable to 0.
Iterate through all the numbers in the array.
Apply the bitwise XOR operator (^) between the result and the current number.
Since identical numbers XOR to 0, all pairs will cancel each other out.
Return the result, which will be the only number that didn't get canceled.

walkthroughSteps: Initializing result to 0 is crucial because 0 XORed with any number is just the number itself.
The XOR operator (^) flips bits. Doing it twice with the same number flips them back to the original state.
XOR is commutative and associative, so the order of the numbers in the array does not matter.
All pairs inherently erase themselves from the 'result' variable.
The algorithm uses purely O(1) space, avoiding hash maps or sets entirely.
commonMistakes: Creating a frequency dictionary, which achieves O(n) time but fails the constant space O(1) constraint.
Trying to use list.count(), creating an extremely slow O(n^2) approach.

title: Remove Element
prompt: Remove all occurrences of a given value from an array in-place. Return the new length of the array. The relative order of elements may be changed.

steps: Initialize a write pointer at index 0.
Iterate through the array using a read pointer.
If the current element is not equal to the target value, copy it to the write pointer's position.
Increment the write pointer.
Return the final write pointer, which represents the new length of the valid items.
approach.example: For [3, 2, 2, 3] target 3. num 3 (skip). num 2 (copy to index 0, write=1). num 2 (copy to index 1, write=2). num 3 (skip). Return 2.

walkthroughSteps: The write_index keeps track of the next available slot for a valid, non-target element.
The loop examines every item sequentially.
When an item shouldn't be removed, it gets placed at the front of the array via the write_index.
The target elements are naturally overwritten without needing costly delete operations.
The final write_index matches exactly how many valid elements were kept.
commonMistakes: Using list.remove(val) in a loop, which shifts all subsequent elements and causes O(n^2) time complexity.
Creating a completely new array, violating the in-place memory constraint.

title: Find the Difference
prompt: You are given two strings s and t. String t is generated by randomizing string s and adding one more letter at a random position. Find the letter that was added.

steps: Initialize a variable to store the XOR sum, starting at 0.
Iterate through all characters in string s, XORing their ASCII integer values into the sum.
Iterate through all characters in string t, XORing their ASCII integer values into the sum.
Since all original characters appear twice, they cancel out to 0. The remaining value is the added character.
Convert the final integer back to a character and return it.
approach.example: s='a', t='aa'. ascii 'a'=97. sum = 0 ^ 97 (from s) ^ 97 (from t) ^ 97 (from t) = 97. chr(97) = 'a'. Return 'a'.

walkthroughSteps: This exploits the property of bitwise XOR where matching elements perfectly cancel each other out.
Python's ord() function translates string characters into their underlying numerical ASCII codes for math operations.
Both strings are processed sequentially, effectively merging their character inventories.
The one character in 't' that doesn't have a partner in 's' is left stranded in the 'result' variable.
The chr() function maps the final numerical value back to the human-readable string character.
commonMistakes: Using a hash map to count characters, which uses O(n) space and requires extra logic to find the mismatched count.
Sorting both strings to compare them sequentially, heavily degrading performance to O(n log n).

title: Isomorphic Strings
prompt: Determine if two strings are isomorphic. Two strings are isomorphic if the characters in the first can be replaced to get the second, preserving order and uniqueness (no two characters map to the same character).

steps: Ensure the strings are the same length; return False if they are not.
Create two empty dictionaries to map characters from s to t, and from t to s.
Iterate through both strings simultaneously.
If a character from s is already mapped to something different, or a character from t is mapped to something different, return False.
Otherwise, register the mapping in both dictionaries.
Return True if the entire string processes successfully.
approach.example: For 'egg', 'add'. 'e'->'a', 'a'->'e'. 'g'->'d', 'd'->'g'. Next 'g', 'g' already maps to 'd', 'd' maps to 'g', matches. Return True.

walkthroughSteps: Two dictionaries are required to ensure a strictly one-to-one mapping in both directions.
The zip() function neatly pairs up corresponding characters from 's' and 't' for the loop.
The first condition checks if 's' is trying to map a letter it previously assigned to a new letter.
The second condition prevents two different letters in 's' from pointing to the same letter in 't'.
If no contradictions are found, the mappings are saved to evaluate future characters.
commonMistakes: Only using one dictionary (e.g., s to t), causing strings like 'bad' and 'bab' to incorrectly register as isomorphic.
Using str.replace() in a loop, which destroys the original string and takes O(n^2) time.

title: Longest Common Prefix
prompt: Find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, return an empty string.

steps: Return an empty string immediately if the input array is empty.
Assume the entire first string is the common prefix.
Iterate through the remaining strings in the array.
While the current string does not start with the assumed prefix, shorten the prefix by one character from the end.
Return the prefix once all strings are checked.
approach.example: For ['flower', 'flow', 'flight']. Prefix='flower'. 'flow' doesn't start with it. Shorten to 'flow'. 'flow' matches. 'flight' doesn't start with 'flow'. Shorten to 'fl'. Matches. Return 'fl'.

walkthroughSteps: The algorithm uses horizontal scanning, taking the first word as the baseline.
The startswith() method checks if the current word contains the exact prefix at the beginning.
Slicing prefix[:-1] removes the last character, progressively making the requirement less strict.
If the prefix shrinks to an empty string, the algorithm aborts early because no commonality exists.
The process repeats, whittling down the prefix until it is valid for every single string.
commonMistakes: Comparing characters vertically index-by-index, which requires careful bounds checking to avoid index out of range errors.
Forgetting to check if the prefix becomes completely empty inside the while loop.

title: Add Binary
prompt: Given two binary strings, return their sum as a binary string.

steps: Initialize two pointers starting at the ends of the two strings, and a carry variable set to 0.
Loop while either pointer is valid or there is a carry to process.
Extract the integer value at the pointers, treating out-of-bounds indices as 0.
Sum the values and the carry, append sum % 2 to a result list, and update the carry to sum // 2.
Reverse the result list and join it into a string to return.
approach.example: For '11' and '1'. End chars 1+1=2. 2%2=0 (append 0), carry=1. Next chars 1+0(out of bounds)+1(carry)=2. append 0, carry=1. Pointers empty, add carry 1. Result ['0','0','1'], reverse to '100'.

code:
def add_binary(a, b):
  result = []
  i = len(a) - 1
  j = len(b) - 1
  carry = 0
  while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
    val_a = int(a[i]) if i >= 0 else 0
    val_b = int(b[j]) if j >= 0 else 0
    total = val_a + val_b + carry
    result.append(str(total % 2))
    carry = total // 2
    i -= 1
    j -= 1
  return ''.join(reversed(result))

walkthroughSteps: The pointers i and j iterate from right to left, matching standard arithmetic addition.
The while condition uniquely ensures the loop continues if a final carry remains after both strings run out.
Ternary conditionals gracefully substitute 0 when one string is shorter than the other.
Modulo 2 dictates what digit is written, while integer division by 2 determines the carry-over.
Because appending to a list builds the number backward, reversing the list at the end formats it properly.
commonMistakes: Converting both strings to decimal, adding them, and converting back to binary. This can overflow maximum integer limits in languages without arbitrary precision.
Forgetting to handle the final carry at the end of the calculation.

title: Pascal's Triangle
prompt: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.

steps: Check if numRows is 0, returning an empty list if so.
Initialize a list of lists, starting with the first row: [[1]].
Start a loop to generate rows from index 1 up to numRows - 1.
For each row, create a temporary array starting and ending with 1, filling the middle elements by summing adjacent elements from the previous row.
Append the newly generated row to the triangle.
approach.example: For 3 rows. Start [[1]]. Row 2: prev is [1], next is [1, 1], add to triangle. Row 3: prev is [1, 1], next is [1, 1+1, 1] = [1, 2, 1], add to triangle.

walkthroughSteps: The base case establishes the absolute tip of the triangle, [[1]].
The outer loop dictates how many total tiers the triangle needs to grow.
triangle[-1] acts as a reference, fetching the immediately preceding row for calculations.
The inner loop runs only for the inner numbers of the current tier, cleanly pulling pairs from the previous row.
The new row is bookended with 1s manually, bypassing out-of-bounds indexing errors entirely.
commonMistakes: Trying to pre-allocate an empty matrix and filling it, which is harder to code cleanly than dynamically appending rows.
Indexing out of bounds when looking up values in prev_row by failing to restrict the inner loop boundaries.

title: Valid Perfect Square
prompt: Determine if a given positive integer is a perfect square. Do not use built-in square root functions like sqrt().

steps: Initialize a binary search with left pointer at 1 and right pointer at the given number.
Loop while the left pointer is less than or equal to the right pointer.
Calculate the midpoint and square it.
If the squared midpoint exactly equals the given number, return True.
Adjust pointers based on if the squared midpoint is too large or too small. Return False if the loop finishes.

walkthroughSteps: Binary search is highly efficient for math problems involving a sorted range of possible integer answers.
The mid is evaluated by squaring it and comparing it to the target number.
If the square is too large, the right boundary is clamped down to eliminate all larger possibilities.
If the square is too small, the left boundary is pushed up.
Exiting the while loop implies the number falls between two whole number squares, making it imperfect.
commonMistakes: Using a for loop to check 1, 2, 3... which triggers a Time Limit Exceeded error on large integers.
Using floats or mathematical exponentiation instead of integer multiplication.

title: Count Words
prompt: Count the number of words in a string without using built-in split functions. Words are separated by one or more spaces, and the string might have leading or trailing spaces.

steps: Initialize a word count variable to 0.
Initialize a boolean flag 'in_word' to False to track if we are currently reading a word.
Iterate through every character in the string.
If the character is a space, set 'in_word' to False.
If it is a non-space and 'in_word' is False, we found a new word: set 'in_word' to True and increment the count.
approach.example: For ' a cat '. char ' ' -> in_word=False. char 'a' -> in_word=True, count=1. char ' ' -> in_word=False. char 'c' -> in_word=True, count=2. count stays 2 through 'a', 't'. End space -> False. Return 2.

walkthroughSteps: The count variable tracks the total number of words found.
The in_word boolean flag acts as a state machine, remembering whether the loop is currently inside a word block.
Spaces immediately break the word state.
When a non-space is found while NOT in a word state, it marks a valid transition into a new word, increasing the count.
Consecutive letters trigger nothing because the state is already in_word, allowing it to gracefully ignore long words.
commonMistakes: Counting spaces to determine word count, which fails completely if there are multiple consecutive spaces.
Failing to account for leading spaces, which could cause an off-by-one error if not handled by a state flag.

title: Matrix Diagonal Sum
prompt: Given a square matrix (a list of lists), calculate the sum of the primary diagonal and the secondary diagonal. Do not count the overlapping center element twice if the matrix has an odd size.

steps: Identify the size of the square matrix (n).
Initialize a sum variable to 0.
Loop from 0 to n-1. In each iteration, add the primary diagonal element at [i][i].
In the same loop, add the secondary diagonal element at [i][n-1-i].
If n is odd, subtract the middle element (at [n//2][n//2]) from the total sum since it was added twice.
approach.example: For 3x3. i=0: add [0][0] and [0][2]. i=1: add [1][1] and [1][1] (overlapping). i=2: add [2][2] and [2][0]. n=3 is odd, subtract [1][1] once. Return sum.

walkthroughSteps: The matrix length n determines both rows and columns because it's a square.
The loop navigates the matrix rows sequentially in a single pass.
mat[i][i] perfectly captures the top-left to bottom-right trajectory.
mat[i][n - 1 - i] perfectly captures the top-right to bottom-left trajectory.
The odd size check dynamically removes the exact center element, correcting the unavoidable double-addition from the loop.
commonMistakes: Using a double nested loop to inspect every matrix element, worsening time complexity from O(n) to O(n^2).
Forgetting to subtract the center element for odd-dimension matrices, resulting in an inflated sum.

title: Find Minimum Value
prompt: Write a function that takes a list of numbers and returns the smallest number. If the list is empty, return None.

steps: Check if the list is empty and return None if it is.
Initialize a variable to store the minimum value, starting with the first element of the list.
Iterate through the remaining elements in the list.
If a current element is smaller than the stored minimum, update the minimum.
Return the final minimum value after checking all elements.
approach.example: For input [4, 2, 7, 1], start with min=4, compare with 2 (new min=2), compare with 7 (min stays 2), compare with 1 (new min=1), return 1.

walkthroughSteps: The edge case of an empty list is handled first to prevent indexing errors.
The variable min_val is seeded with the first item in the list.
A for loop visits every number in the list sequentially.
The conditional checks if the current number beats the current min_val.
Once the loop finishes, min_val holds the absolute smallest number seen.
commonMistakes: Initializing the minimum value to 0, which fails if the list contains only positive numbers greater than 0.
Forgetting to check for an empty list, leading to an IndexError on nums[0].

title: Count Vowels
prompt: Create a function that counts and returns the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in a given string. The function should be case-insensitive.

steps: Define a set of all vowel characters in both lowercase and uppercase.
Initialize a counter variable to track the number of vowels found.
Iterate through each character in the input string.
If the character exists in the vowel set, increment the counter.
Return the final count.
approach.example: For input 'Apple', check 'A' (count=1), 'p' (count=1), 'p' (count=1), 'l' (count=1), 'e' (count=2), returning 2.

walkthroughSteps: A set is created to hold all valid vowel characters for rapid O(1) lookups.
The count variable begins at zero.
The for loop processes the string one character at a time.
The membership test 'in' checks the set, incrementing count when a match is found.
The total count is returned after the entire string is evaluated.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to handle uppercase vowels, causing 'A' to be missed.
Using a list instead of a set for vowels, which is technically slower for lookups (though negligible for 10 items).

title: Check Palindrome
prompt: Write a function that returns True if a given string reads the same forwards and backwards, and False otherwise.

steps: Initialize two pointers: one at the start of the string, and one at the end.
Loop while the left pointer is less than the right pointer.
If the characters at the pointers do not match, return False.
Move the left pointer forward and the right pointer backward.
If the loop finishes without finding mismatches, return True.
approach.example: For input 'racecar', compare 'r' and 'r' (match), move inward to 'a' and 'a' (match), move inward to 'c' and 'c' (match), loop ends, return True.

walkthroughSteps: The left and right pointers are positioned at opposite ends of the string.
The while loop continues as long as the pointers haven't crossed paths.
The character comparison immediately exits with False if a mismatch is detected.
The pointers are updated to step towards the center of the string.
Reaching the end of the loop means all mirrored characters matched perfectly.
commonMistakes: Using a for loop over the entire string length and doing redundant checks after crossing the midpoint.
Off-by-one errors when setting the initial right pointer to len(s) instead of len(s) - 1.

title: Sum of Squares

  operator = '+'

  return total + value if operator == '+' else total - value

steps: Traverse the tree in preorder.
Store a marker for missing children.
Join the traversal values into a string.
Use the same preorder sequence to reconstruct the tree.
approach.example: For a root 1 with left child 2 and no right child, serialization preserves the missing-child marker so the original structure can be reconstructed.

walkthroughSteps: serialize records every node and every missing child.
The missing-child marker preserves tree structure.
deserialize consumes values in the same preorder order.
Each non-marker value creates a node and recursively builds its children.
commonMistakes: Skipping null children during serialization and losing structural information.
Using a different traversal order during deserialization.

title: Graph Clone
prompt: Given a connected graph node, create a deep copy of the entire graph while preserving all connections.

steps: Use a dictionary to map original nodes to their copies.
Create a copy when an original node is first visited.
Recursively clone every neighbor.
Attach each cloned neighbor to the copied node.
approach.example: For a graph where node 1 connects to nodes 2 and 3, cloning creates separate copies of 2 and 3 and connects them to the copy of 1.

walkthroughSteps: copies prevents repeatedly cloning the same graph node.
A copy is stored before its neighbors are processed.
Each neighbor is recursively cloned and attached to the copy.
Cycles are handled because previously seen nodes are returned from copies.
commonMistakes: Creating a new copy every time a node is encountered.
Storing the copy only after recursively visiting neighbors, which breaks on cycles.

title: Dijkstra Shortest Path
prompt: Given a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights and a starting node, return the shortest distance from the start to every node.

steps: Initialize every distance as infinity except the start.
Use a priority queue to select the closest unprocessed node.
Relax each outgoing edge.
Push improved distances back into the priority queue.
approach.example: For edges where 0 connects to 1 with weight 4 and to 2 with weight 1, the algorithm first reaches 2 cheaply and can then use it to improve paths to other nodes.

walkthroughSteps: distances stores the best known distance to every node.
The heap always exposes the smallest currently known distance.
An edge is relaxed when traveling through the current node gives a shorter path.
Stale heap entries are ignored when they no longer match distances.
commonMistakes: Using Dijkstra with negative edge weights.
Failing to ignore stale priority queue entries.

title: Union Find Connectivity
prompt: Given a number of nodes and undirected connections, determine whether two specified nodes belong to the same connected component.

steps: Initialize every node as its own parent.
Find the root representative of each node.
Union the roots when a connection joins different components.
Compare the roots of the two requested nodes.
approach.example: For connections [(0,1), (1,2)] nodes 0 and 2 share the same component, so checking their roots returns true.

walkthroughSteps: Each node initially belongs to its own component.
find returns the representative root of a component.
union combines two different components using their roots.
Path compression and union by size keep the structure shallow.
commonMistakes: Connecting nodes directly without finding their roots.
Forgetting path compression or component-size balancing in the implementation.

title: Edit Distance
prompt: Given two strings, return the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and replacements needed to transform the first string into the second.

steps: Create a dynamic programming table for prefixes of both strings.
Initialize empty-string transformation costs.
Keep the previous diagonal value when characters match.
Otherwise choose the cheapest insertion, deletion, or replacement.
approach.example: For 'horse' and 'ros', changing horse through replacement and deletion operations requires three edits in total.

walkthroughSteps: previous stores edit costs for the previous row of the table.
A matching pair needs no new operation and uses the diagonal value.
A mismatch can be solved by insertion, deletion, or replacement.
Only the previous row is required, reducing memory usage.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong neighboring values for insertion and deletion.
Forgetting that matching characters should copy the diagonal result without adding one.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
prompt: Given a list of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

steps: Maintain a list of the smallest possible tail value for each subsequence length.
Use binary search to locate where each number belongs.
Replace an existing tail when the current number is smaller.
The length of the tails list is the answer.
approach.example: For [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18], a longest increasing subsequence has length 4, such as [2,3,7,101].

walkthroughSteps: tails[index] stores the smallest tail known for a subsequence of length index plus one.
bisect_left finds the first tail that is not smaller than the current value.
A smaller tail gives future values more room to extend the subsequence.
The number of stored tails equals the maximum subsequence length.
commonMistakes: Using bisect_right and accidentally allowing equal values in a strictly increasing sequence.
Interpreting tails itself as the actual longest subsequence.

title: Partition Equal Subset
prompt: Given a list of positive integers, determine whether it can be divided into two subsets with equal sums.

steps: Calculate the total sum.
Return false when the total is odd.
Use a set of reachable subset sums up to half the total.
Check whether the target half sum becomes reachable.
approach.example: For [1,5,11,5], the total is 22 and the target is 11, which can be formed by 11 or by 5 plus 5 plus 1, so the list can be partitioned.

walkthroughSteps: An equal partition requires each subset to sum to half of the total.
An odd total cannot be split into two equal integer sums.
reachable stores sums that can be formed using processed values.
The target being reachable means an equal partition exists.
commonMistakes: Continuing when the total sum is odd.
Reusing the same number multiple times within one iteration.

title: Maximum Subarray Product
prompt: Given a list of integers, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product.

steps: Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at the current position.
Swap them when the current number is negative.
Extend the current products or start a new subarray.
Track the largest product seen.
approach.example: For [2,3,-2,4], the subarray [2,3] has product 6, which is larger than every other contiguous product.

walkthroughSteps: A negative number can turn a very small negative product into a large positive product.
maximum and minimum therefore both need to be tracked.
The values are swapped before multiplication when the current number is negative.
best records the largest product ending at any position.
commonMistakes: Tracking only the maximum product and losing useful negative products.
Resetting the product whenever a negative number appears.

title: Kth Largest Element
prompt: Given an unsorted list of integers and k, return the kth largest value without fully sorting the list.

steps: Use a min-heap containing the largest k values seen so far.
Add each number to the heap.
Remove the smallest heap value when the heap grows beyond k.
The remaining smallest heap value is the kth largest value.
approach.example: For [3,2,1,5,6,4] with k equal to 2, the two largest values are 6 and 5, so the second largest value is 5.

walkthroughSteps: The heap stores only the k largest values encountered so far.
The smallest value inside that heap represents the current kth largest value.
When a new value makes the heap too large, the smallest value is removed.
After all values are processed, heap[0] is the kth largest value.
commonMistakes: Using a max-heap and removing the largest value.
Keeping more than k elements and unnecessarily increasing memory use.

title: LRU Cache
prompt: Implement a least recently used cache that supports constant-time get and put operations while removing the least recently used item when capacity is exceeded.

steps: Use a dictionary for constant-time key lookup.
Use a doubly linked list to track usage order.
Move accessed or inserted nodes to the most recently used position.
Remove the least recently used node when capacity is exceeded.
approach.example: For a cache of capacity 2, inserting keys 1 and 2 then accessing 1 makes 1 recent, so inserting key 3 removes key 2.

walkthroughSteps: The dictionary maps keys directly to their linked-list nodes.
The doubly linked list stores nodes from least recently used to most recently used.
get moves an accessed node to the most recently used position.
put removes the least recently used node when capacity is exceeded.
commonMistakes: Updating the dictionary without removing the old linked-list node.
Removing the most recently used node instead of the least recently used node.
